title: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and the language debate: should African fiction be written in English?
group: BLIT-POST — Postcolonial and world literatures in English

left.title: Ngũgĩ: mother tongue
points: Write in Gikuyu for the people

explain.say: Imagine being punished at school for speaking your own language, made to wear a sign around your neck calling you stupid. That happened to the Kenyan writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and his classmates. Years later it fuelled one of the great debates in world literature. The board shows the two sides.

left.title: Ngũgĩ: mother tongue
points: Write in Gikuyu for the people

explain.say: Follow his path. In 1962 he attended a famous conference of African writers at Makerere University in Uganda, and his first novels were in English. Then in 1977 he co-wrote a play in Gikuyu performed by villagers, and the Kenyan government jailed him without trial for a year. Why would a play in a local language frighten a government?

events.ask: What is Decolonising the Mind about?

explain.say: In prison he drafted a novel in Gikuyu on toilet paper, later published as Devil on the Cross. In 1986, in Decolonising the Mind, he said farewell to English for his fiction, arguing that language carries a people's memory, and writing in a colonial language keeps the mind colonised. Do you agree a language carries a way of seeing?

events.ask: What is Decolonising the Mind about?

explain.say: Now the other side. Chinua Achebe argued that English, though forced on Africa, could be reshaped to carry African experience: a new English, bent to fit African life. Nigeria has over five hundred languages, and English let writers reach all of them, and the world. Which side persuades you?

left.title: Ngũgĩ: mother tongue
points: Write in Gikuyu for the people

explain.say: The debate is still alive. Look at the reasons: who can read the book, which languages publishers pay for, and what translation can carry. Ngũgĩ kept writing in Gikuyu and translating his work into English, so in a way he chose both. Great work. Challenge: write one sentence in your first language that loses something in English.

faq.q: Why did Ngũgĩ stop writing in English?
faq.a: He came to see English as a tool of colonial control that cut Africans off from their own culture and from ordinary readers. Writing in Gikuyu, he could reach peasants and workers and help decolonise the mind.
asks: Why does Ngũgĩ write in Gikuyu?

faq.q: What did Achebe think about writing in English?
faq.a: In his 1965 essay The African Writer and the English Language, Achebe argued that English could be adapted to express African experience, creating a new English shaped by African speech and proverbs.

faq.q: What is Decolonising the Mind about?
faq.a: Ngũgĩ's 1986 book of essays argues that colonialism worked through language, teaching African children to despise their mother tongues, and announces his decision to write fiction only in Gikuyu.

The 1962 Conference of African Writers of English Expression at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda. Achebe, Wole Soyinka and the young Ngũgĩ attended, and it sparked the question of which languages count as African literature.
After the 1977 play Ngaahika Ndeenda, I Will Marry When I Want, performed in Gikuyu by villagers at Kamiriithu, criticised Kenya's elite, the government detained him without trial for about a year.

facts: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o (1938–2025) was born in Kenya and first published under the name James Ngugi.
He was detained without trial from December 1977 to December 1978.
His essay collection Decolonising the Mind was published in 1986.
